candidates.attacker_control: Any user-controlled URL value that reaches XSSAPI.getValidHref() (or XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref()) — e.g. a link target saved in content or reflected from a request parameter — can be supplied as `javascript:alert(document.domain)` (or any other obfuscated dangerous-scheme payload).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified that numeric entity (`:`, `:`) and the five XML entity forms are decoded during validation and therefore rejected, and that a literal ':' is rejected by both onsiteURL (colon absent from the class) and offsiteURL (requires an http/https/ftp/mailto prefix), so the classic `javascript:` and `:` forms do not work. Also verified the percent-encoding of quotes/angle brackets/backtick/space, so raw attribute breakout is not possible. The residual attack depends on the value being emitted without additional HTML-escaping of '&' (a downstream engine that re-encodes '&' as '&' would neutralize it); the javadoc for getValidHref indicates direct attribute use, which is the unsanitized case. It was not possible to inspect AntiSamy/Johnzon/ESAPI internals (provided dependencies, not in the snapshot), so the exact match semantics of AntiSamy `Attribute.containsAllowedValue`/`matchesAllowedExpression` and the resolution of the `<a>` tag's `<attribute name="href"/>` (config.xml:807) against `<common-attributes>` (config.xml:243-248) rest on the Sling code comment mirroring MagicSAXFilter rather than direct inspection.
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting (arbitrary script execution in the victim's session, e.g. on click of an attacker-supplied link) in exactly the context the XSS Protection API is meant to secure. The bug is in the sanitizer itself, not in an unusual caller usage: the API contract promises an attribute-safe/sanitized URL and the value is embedded raw by design.
candidates.prerequisites: The caller writes the returned string directly into an href/src attribute without further HTML-encoding, which is the documented purpose of the method ("Sanitizes a URL for writing as an HTML href or src attribute value"); the method itself percent-encodes quotes, angle brackets, backtick and space precisely so it can be emitted as-is. The victim's browser must parse the attribute value as HTML (normal case) so that `:` is decoded to ':'.
candidates.root_cause: URL sanitization decodes only percent-encoding (URLDecoder) and XML entities (StringEscapeUtils.unescapeXml: the five predefined XML entities plus numeric references). Validation is then a whole-string whitelist (AntiSamy onsiteURL) whose character class deliberately permits '&', ';', '(', ')' for query strings. Named HTML5 character references such as `:` are not XML entities, so they are neither decoded during validation nor percent-encoded in the output. The result is that the returned string can still contain an HTML-character-reference-obfuscated scheme separator that the browser decodes when the value is placed in an attribute, defeating the javascript:-scheme check.
candidates.title: getValidHref() accepts undeclared HTML5 named entities, allowing javascript: scheme smuggling into href/src attributes
candidates.trace: 1) getValidHref(url) percent-decodes the input (XSSAPIImpl.java:232) and XML-unescapes it (line 237); `:` is untouched by both. 2) Only `"`, `'`, `>`, `<`, backtick and space are percent-encoded (lines 241-246); '&' and ';' are preserved. 3) isValidHref(encodedUrl) (XSSFilterImpl.java:127-146) percent-decodes and XML-unescapes again, yielding the same string, so runHrefValidation() is applied to `javascript:alert(1)`. 4) hrefAttribute.containsAllowedValue(...) matches the AntiSamy onsiteURL pattern (XSSFilterImpl.java:75 / config.xml:70), whose character class includes letters, '&', ';', '(' and ')' and contains no colon, so the value is accepted even though the literal-colon forms (`javascript:alert(1)`, `:`, `:`) are correctly rejected. 5) getValidHref returns the accepted string unchanged; written into `<a href="...">`, the HTML tokenizer decodes `:` to ':' and the browser navigates to/executes javascript:alert(1) when the link is activated.
candidates.unverified: Not executed or dynamically reproduced (no code/tests/scanners run). Browser-side decoding of `:` in attribute values is background HTML knowledge, not verified in this run. Whether the AntiSamy attribute lookup anchors the whole string and which href regexps are actually bound to the `a` tag cannot be confirmed from the snapshot because the AntiSamy library is a provided dependency.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS); incomplete entity decoding in URL validation (CWE-79/CWE-20)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 17 files, all indexed and readable (no binary/sensitive/symlink exclusions, no unindexed files). Read in full: XSSAPIImpl.java, XSSFilterImpl.java, HtmlToHtmlContentContext.java, PlainTextToHtmlContentContext.java, PolicyHandler.java, XSSFilterRule.java, LongValidationRule.java, ProtectionContext.java, XSSAPI.java, pom.xml, README.md, validation.properties. Read partially/searched: config.xml (2818-line AntiSamy policy; common-regexps/directives, common-attributes, tag definitions for a/img/style/script/iframe/meta/form/object/link read or searched), ESAPI.properties (searched canonicalization/encoder/validator/crypto settings), XSSFilter.java (lines 1-60; final ~13 lines not read), .gitignore and package-info.java not read. Relation index: complete (17/17 files, 232 calls, 132 symbols, 4 facts); used only for navigation, and its JSON 'security_call' labels were independently checked in source. No tests exist in the snapshot, so no test-driven confirmation was possible.
limitations: No code, tests, scanners or payloads were executed; all conclusions are static source analysis.

AntiSamy 1.5.2, ESAPI 2.1.0, OWASP Encoder 1.1.1 and Johnzon are provided dependencies and are not present in the snapshot, so attribute-matching semantics, HTML parsing behavior of AntiSamy's scanner, and generator escaping behavior could not be verified from source.
The behavior of a browser decoding HTML5 named character references such as `:` in attribute values is background knowledge, not demonstrated in this run.
config.xml was reviewed selectively (targeted reads/searches of ~600 of 2818 lines); unrelated policy rules were not exhaustively audited.
XSSFilter.java lines 61-73, .gitignore and package-info.java were not read; no conclusion is drawn about them.
The relation index does not prove reachability or data flow, so caller-side reachability of getValidHref() in a deployed Sling/AEM instance is inferred from the public API contract, not traced.

rejected_leads.lead: getValidMultiLineComment() only rejects `*/` (XSSAPIImpl.java:353-359) although its javadoc says it is for use inside `<script>...</script>`/`<style>...</style>` (XSSAPI.java:132-140); an input containing `</script>` (no `*/`) would terminate the script element in the HTML parser and permit markup/script injection.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible script-element breakout, but the documented contract only states that the comment-end block is disallowed and does not promise HTML-parser safety; exploitability depends on the caller concatenating `/*` + value + `*/` into a script element. Weaker contract violation than the chosen candidate, so not submitted.

rejected_leads.lead: getValidJSON() and getValidXML() return re-serialized/original strings that may contain raw '<', '>' or `</script>` (XSSAPIImpl.java:365-417); the relation index flagged the Json reader calls at lines 378/386 as security calls.
rejected_leads.reason: The javadoc promises only 'a valid JSON string'/'a valid XML string', not HTML/script-context safety; embedder misuse is required. Index labels are name-based navigation hints and were not treated as evidence.

rejected_leads.lead: PlainTextToHtmlContentContext.escapeXml() escapes only '&', '<', '>' (PlainTextToHtmlContentContext.java:50-69) while ProtectionContext documents OWASP rule #1 (quotes included).
rejected_leads.reason: The context is explicitly HTML element content, where escaping '&', '<', '>' is the correct and sufficient rule; quotes are only required in attribute contexts, so no source-evidenced XSS.

rejected_leads.lead: getValidStyleToken()/getValidCSSColor() admit constructs such as `expression(...)`, backslash escapes inside url(...) (XSSAPIImpl.java:284-348), and the embedded AntiSamy policy pins on* event attributes to the literals `javascript:void(0)`/`javascript:history.go(-1)` (config.xml:399-450).
rejected_leads.reason: No modern-browser execution path could be established from source; the on* literal values are inert and are standard AntiSamy policy content, and the CSS constructs are legacy/IE-only speculative leads.

rejected_leads.lead: Policy loading uses the relative path DEFAULT_POLICY_PATH='sling/xss/config.xml' with a service resource resolver and an endsWith() change filter (XSSFilterImpl.java:82-109, 216-257), which could load an attacker-planted policy if a search-path location is writable.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires write privileges on /apps or another search-path location (privileged attacker), and the change filter reloads only the resolved default path, not the changed path; no attacker-controlled path was demonstrated.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Sling XSS bundle snapshot (17 files: XSSAPI/XSSFilter APIs, impl classes, AntiSamy policy config.xml, ESAPI/validation properties, pom). The strongest source-evidenced candidate is in the URL sanitizer: getValidHref()/isValidHref() decode only percent-encoding and XML entities before applying the AntiSamy onsiteURL/offsiteURL whitelist, which explicitly allows '&' and ';'. HTML5 named character references (e.g. `:`) are neither decoded nor encoded away, so an input such as `javascript:alert(1)` passes validation and is returned verbatim to be written into an href/src attribute, where the browser's HTML tokenizer decodes `:` back to ':' and executes the javascript: URL. Other plausible but weaker leads (script-element breakout via getValidMultiLineComment, raw '<'/'>' in getValidJSON/getValidXML output, quote handling in PLAIN_HTML_CONTENT, CSS token validator) are recorded as rejected or unconfirmed rather than as additional candidates.
